In gen., of buildings: conclave illud concidit,: navis veluti terrestre machinamentum,: turris terrae motu,; cf.: urbs acerbissimo concidat incendio conflagrata,.—Of other objects: omne caelum,: ipse et equus ejus ante signum Jovis concidit,: (alces) infirmas arbores pondere adfligunt atque unā ipsae concidunt,: pinus bipenni Thessalā,: ad terram pondere vasto,: sub onere,: pronus in fimo,—

la:verb:concedo.gloss: to depart, retire or withdraw, come away, come, go away
senses: to depart, retire or withdraw, come away, come, go away
to relinquish, concede, relent, subside, come to an end, terminate, give up, abandon
to grant or allow, allow, yield, grant, concede
la:verb:concedo.html:
con-cēdo, cessi, cessum, 3, v. n. and a.
(a strengthened cedo, and corresp. with it in most of its signiff.); lit., to go, walk; hence,
Neutr., with reference to the terminus a quo, to go or walk away from a place, to depart, retire, withdraw, remove from (in lit. signif. rare but class.).
In gen.: concedite atque abscedite omnes, de viā decedite,; so absol., ; ; cf.: ipsae concedite silvae,farewell,.—With prep.: a foribus,: abs te,: ab oculis alicujus,: superis ab oris,: ex aedibus,.—With abl. only: oculis,: caelo,: solio,.—With adv.: hinc,; ; .—
Esp.
Pregn. ( = cedo, II. A. 2.), to pass away, disappear, vanish, in Tac. (with and without vitā), to depart from life, die: tumor et irae Concessere deūm,: vitā,to die,; ; ; 12, 39; 14, 51; and absol.: quandoque concessero, ; 13, 30; the same: concessit superis ab oris,; cf.: vitā per auras concessit ad Manes,. —
With dat. or absol., prop. qs. to go out of the way for one (on account of his wishes, or his superior power or excellence), i. e. to yield to, submit, give way to, adapt one's self to.
To yield or submit to power or compulsion: ut magnitudini medicinae doloris magnitudo concederet,: certum est, concedere homini nato nemini,: neque nox quoquam concedit die (i. e. diei), (cf. ): cedant arma togae, concedat laurea linguae, Cic. Poët. Off. 1, 22, 77 (cf. , and ): bellum ac tumultum paci atque otio concessurum,: voluptatem concessuram dignitati,: injuriae,: obsidioni,i. e. permit,: operi meo concedite,; : naturae,i. e. to die,; so, fato,: fatis magnis,: apparebat aut hostibus aut civibus de victoriā concedendum esse,; cf. so impers.: postquam concessum propemodum de victoriā credebant,.—
To give place to in excellence, dignity, rank, etc., to yield to, to give precedence: me amantissimum tui, nemini concedentem,; so ; 4, 3, 4: etsi de cupiditate nemini concedam,: sese unis Suebis concedere,: majestati ejus viri concedere,: aetati,; ; cf. so impers.: Sulla, cujus facundiae, non aetati a Manlio concessum,: vigenti Silio,: seniori Sentio,: ut vix Apronio illi de familiaritate concedere videatur,: Antario Varoque de gloriā,: nemini in illa causā studio et cupiditate concedere,: nec amore in hanc patriam nobis concedunt,: nec, si muneribus certes, concedat Iollas,.—With acc. of quantity (cf. 3. infra): magistro tantulum de arte,: alicui quicquam in desperatione,. —
To yield, submit to one's will, comply with one's wishes: ut tibi concedam, neque tuae libidini advorsabor,: matri meae,: concessit senatus postulationi tuae,: jurisconsultis concedi,.— Impers.: Caesar ... concedendum non putabat,.—
Like συγχωρεῖν τινι, to assent to, concede to: nunquamne hodie concedes mihi Neque intelleges, etc., (credes, consenties, Ruhnk.): stultum me fateor, liceat concedere veris, (cf. in Gr. συγχωρεῖν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ).—
To assent to, grant, pardon, allow, etc.: quos (judices) alienis peccatis concessuros putes, quo facilius ipsis peccare liceat,: poëtae non ignoscit, nobis concedit,: dicto concedi,: cui (vitio) si concedere nolis,; cf. .—Hence (cf. cedo, II. A. 3. fin.),
Act., with acc. (and dat.) aliquid alicui.
To grant, concede, allow; to consign something over to, to resign, yield, vouchsafe, confirm to, etc. (very freq. in all perr. and species of composition): illum mihi aequius est quam me illi quae volo concedere,: si nunc de tuo jure concessisses paululum,: partem octavam pretii,: date hoc et concedite pudori meo, ut, etc.,; cf. : alicui primas in dicendo partis,: amicis quicquid velint,: neque quicquam illius audaciae,: doctrinam alicui,; cf.: artes tibi,: intellegentiam, prudentiam,: principatum imperii maritimi Atheniensibus,; cf. id. Dion, 6, 3; ; ; ; cf.: tempus quieti, aut luxuriae,: tempestivum pueris ludum,: libertatem his,: vitam alicui,; ; : crimen gratiae, i. e. to accuse or inform against for the sake of favor, : peccata alicui,to pardon him,: delicta,.—Pass.: Siciliam nimis celeri desperatione rerum concessam,

had been ceded, given up, : Scaevolae concessa est facundiae virtus,; et saep.: acrius ... Ulcisci, quam nunc concessum est legibus aequis,; cf. ; .—Poet., with in and acc.: concessit in iras Ipse ... genitor Calydona Dianae,gave over to be punished,.—

With dat. and inf.: nec nostrā dicere linguā Concedit nobis patrii sermonis egestas,; so, ducere neptem,: esse poëtis,; et saep.—Impers. pass.: de re publicā nisi per concilium loqui non conceditur,: quo mihi fortunam, si non conceditur uti,; ; ; ; : servis quoque pueros hujus aetatis verberare concedimus,: concedunt plangere matri,: cum accusare etiam palam concessum sit,; ; : 8, 3, 30; 12, 3, 8 al.—Poet.: fatis numquam concessa moveri Camarina,not allowed. forbidden to be removed,; cf. also personally: haec ubi conceduntur esse facta, for conceditur haec esse facta,.—
With acc. and inf.: non omnia corpora vocem Mittere concedis,you grant,: oculos falli,; : culpam inesse concedam,: poëtas legendos oratori futuro,.—Pass. impers.: concedatur profecto verum esse, ut, etc.,. —
With ut or ne: nec vero histrionibus oratoribusque concedendum est, ut iis haec apta sint, nobis dissoluta,: verum concedo tibi ut ea praetereas, quae, etc.,: concedant ut viri boni fuerint,; ; : non concedo, ut sola sint,: cui concedi potest, ut? etc., ap. : ut concedatur ne in conspectum veniat,.—(ε) With a simple subj.: concedo sit dives,; . —(ζ) Absol.: beatos esse deos sumpsisti: concedimus,; ; cf. : consules neque concedebant neque valde repugnabant,; .—
= condono, to grant or yield something to one as a favor or from regard, to desist from, forbear, give up; forgive, pardon: inimicitias rei publicae,to give up for the sake of the State,: petitionem alicui,from regard to,: peccata liberum parentum misericordiae,: cum Marcellum senatui reique publicae concessisti,: ut concessisti illum (sc. Marcellum) senatui, sic da hunc (sc. Ligarium) populo,as you have pardoned him in deference to the Senate,; cf. ; ; : Montanus patri concessus est,fin.
Neutr., in respect to the terminus ad quem, to go, walk, betake one's self somewhere, to retire, withdraw to, etc.; with ad, in, or adv.: tantisper hic ego ad januam concessero, Wagn.; cf.: ad Manes,i. e. to die,: ad victorem,: ad dexteram,: caeli distributio docet unde fulmen venerit, quo concesserit,; so : huc,; ; ; ; Caecil. ap. : istuc,; : vis animae in altum,: in delubrum,: in hiberna,; cf.: Carthaginem Novam in hiberna,: Argos habitatum,: Cythnum,: Neapolin,: Patavium,: in insulam,: in turbam,: trans Rhenum,: concede huc a foribus,: hinc intro,; : hinc aliquo ab ore eorum,; cf.: aliquo ab eorum oculis,: hinc rus,.—
Trop.: in aliquid, of entering into an alliance, yielding to, etc., to agree or consent to, to assent, to submit, yield, or resign one's self, to acquiesce in, to go or pass over to any thing (freq. in the histt.): mulier, conjuncta viro, concessit in unum Conubium,; cf.: in matrimonium,: victi omnes in gentem nomenque imperantium concessere, were merged in, passed over into, ; so, in paucorum potentium jus atque dicionem,; cf.: in dicionem,: in dominationem, Gerl.: in deditionem,; ; : in Tyrias leges,: in condiciones,: in sententiam,; ; ; cf.: in illos, assent to, yield to them, ap. Aug. contr. Av: in partes,.

la:verb:concludo.html:
con-clūdo, si, sum, 3 (
part. perf. solecist. conclausa semina, ), v. a., to shut up closely, to close up, enclose, confine.
Prop. (class. in prose and poetry), constr. with in and acc., with adv. and absol. (not with in and abl., for the true read., , is inclusit): in vincla bestiam nequissimam,; cf.: bestias delectationis causā, Madv.: eos concludit, magnam hominum multitudinem,: quia enim in caveā si forent Conclussi itidem ut pulli gallinacei,: conclusam hic habeo uxorem saevam,: aliquem in fenestram,: me in cellam cum illā,; cf.: in aediculam,: illum aliquo,: locum sulco,: at tu conclusas hircinis follibus auras ... imitare,: piscina conclusa porticibus,: Tigris et Euphrates Mesopotamiam ab utroque latere concludunt,: vulnera cerā,: venti procella conclusa,: concluso loco,: primordia conclusa,: suave locus voci resonat conclusus,: conclusa aqua (opp.: profluens amnis),; cf.: longe aliam esse navigationem concluso mari atque in vastissimo,: coagmentis ad centrum respondentibus fornices concluduntur,: statio conclusa atque munita,.—
Humorously: non placet qui amicos intra dentis conclusos habet,.—
Trop.
To include, compress, restrain, comprise: omnia fere, quae sunt conclusa nunc artibus, dispersa et dissipata quondam fuerunt,: fortuna tot res, in unum conclusit diem,: ut ab illā excludar, huc concludar,i. e. I shall be fettered by this marriage, (ex ferarum translatione concludar dixit, Don.); : concludere jus civile in parvum et angustum locum,; ; : uno hoc volumine vitam excellentium virorum complurium,; cf.: in hanc formulam omnia judicia,: eidem et infinitam largitionem remittebas et eundem in angustissimam formulam sponsionis concludebas?: istum locum in unam speciem,.—
(Cf. claudo, I. B.) To end, close, conclude: facinus natum a cupiditate, auctum per stuprum, crudelitate perfectum atque conclusum,: (ancipites variique casus) exitu notabili concluduntur,: provincia in quā laus equitatis, integritatis, facilitatis ad extremum ludorum voluptate concluditur,: vitam,.—Esp., of letters, speech, the written or spoken treatment of any subject, etc.: epistulam,: crimen decumanum,: ad illa redeamus eaque ipsa concludamus aliquando,: perorationem,.—
In rhet., of discourse, to close rhythmically, to round off: verborum ordinem alias aliā terminatione,: sententias,; cf. : concludam si potero Latine; Graecum enim hunc versum nostis omnes,: sensum non expleto numero,; cf. and 125: verbum acuto tenore (just before: acuto sono finiant),: versum,.—
In philos. t. t., to conclude, infer, make an inference, to argue, demonstrate; with acc.: singulas argumentationes,; cf. argumentum,; : argumentum ratione,: quomodo efficiatur concludaturque ratio,: id quod concludere illi velint, non effici ex propositis, nec esse consequens, : ex rebus concessis concludi quod velis,.—With acc. and inf.: deinde concludebas, summum malum esse dolorem, etc.,; cf. .—Absol.: concludere hoc modo: si sunt di, etc.,: ea sumunt ad concludendum, quorum iis nihil conceditur,; ; ; ; 12, 2, 25.—Hence, P. a.: con-clūsus, a, um, confined, closed, in comp.: locus conclusior,.—Subst.: conclūsum, i, n. (acc. to II. D.), a conclusion in a syllogism, .— Advv.
conclūdenter, by consequence, consequently, Boëth. Arist. Elench. Soph. 1, 10, p. 744.—*
conclūsē (acc. to II. C.), with periods rhetorically rounded, harmoniously: concluse apteque dicere,.

la:verb:concurro.gloss: to run with others, flock together
senses: to run with others, flock together
to meet, clash, dash together, strike one another
la:verb:concurro.html:
con-curro, curri, cursum, 3 (
perf. redupl. concucurrit, Duker N. cr.: concucurrisse, Cato ap. P., and ; cf. Oud., and Ind. Flor. s. h. v. Duker), v. n.
To run together (of several persons), to come or assemble together in multitudes, to rush or flock together in crowds (very freq., and class.).
Prop.
Absol.: tota Italia concurret,: video hac tempestate concurrisse omnis adversarios, Cato ap. P.: concurrunt jussu meo plures uno tempore librarii,: cum omnes, ut mos est, concurrerent,: licet concurrant omnes plebei philosophi, nihil tam eleganter explicabunt, etc.,unite,: multi concurrerant,; : concurrite, concurrite, cives,.—Impers.: contionem inprimis advocari jubet; summā cum expectatione concurritur,.—
Designating the place from which, or the place or purpose to or for which: non solum qui in urbe erant, sed etiam undique ex agris concurrerunt,: undique gentes,: concurrunt laeti mi obviam cupedinarii omnes,: ad hos (sc. Druides) magnus adulescentium numerus disciplinae causā concurrit, ; cf. : ad eum magnae copiae,: ad eum homines omnium ordirum corruptissimi, Dietsch: ad curiam, (corresp. to convolare ad Rostra); ; : domum tuam cuncta civitas,: ad arma milites,; so fin.: ad non dubiam mortem,: ad auxilium sociae,: signum dedit, ut ad me restituendum Romam concurrerent,: omnes concurrerunt ad Perdiccam opprimendum,united together,; : ad aliquem audiendum,. —Impers.: concurritur undique ad commune incendium restinguendum,: concurrendum ad curiam putare,: cum ad arma concurri oporteret,: ex proximis castellis eo concursum est,: concursum ad curiam esse,: ; .—*
Poet., to run in attendance upon, to accompany: est quibus Eleae concurrit palma quadrigae, as it were,follows him on foot, accompanies, (4, 8), 17.—
Trop. = confugere, to run for refuge or help, to take refuge (rare): ad C. Aquilium, B. and K.: nulla sedes, quo concurrant,: ne darem perditis civibus hominem, quo concurrerent,: interea servitia repudiabat (Catilina), opibus conjurationis fretus,; .—
Of words, as under military command: ante enim circumscribitur mente sententia confestimque verba concurrunt, quae mens eadem ... statim dimittit, ut suo quodque loco respondeat,.—
To run upon one another, to meet or dash together (class.).
Of corporeal objects.
In gen.: concurrunt nubes ventis,; cf. : ne prorae concurrerent, (al. prorā; cf. Weissenb. ad loc.); cf. ; : mediis concurrere in undis (montes, viz., the Symplegades),; cf. : concurrere montes duo inter se,: actor cum stetit in scaenā, concurrit dextera laevae (viz., in applauding), : labra concurrunt,draw together, close,: os concurrit, id. Ira, 3, 15, 1; : os,; .—Transf., of letters and words: aspere concurrunt litterae, (opp. diduci); so .—Hence,
In partic., milit. t. t., to rush together in hostility, to engage in combat, to join battle, to fight (most freq. in the histt.); constr. inter se, cum aliquo, adversus, in, contra aliquem, alicui, and absol.
Inter se: concurrunt equites inter se,; so ; ; ; ; .—
Cum aliquo: cum hoc concurrit ipse Eumenes,; so ; ; ; .—
Adversus, in, or contra aliquem: recenti milite adversus fessos longo itinere concurrerat, Weissenb. ad loc.: in aliquem,; : equites contra tantam multitudinem audacissime concurrunt, run upon, against, etc., Auct. B. Afr. 6.—
Alicui (freq. in the poets): audet viris concurrere virgo,; ; ; : quibus (equitibus) cum inpigre, Numidae concurrissent, Weissenb. ad loc.—(ε) Absol.: repente Antonius in aciem suas copias de vico produxit et sine morā concurrit, Galb. ap. : cum infestis signis concurrunt,; so ; ; ; ; : ex insidiis,; : mutuis vulneribus,.—Impers. pass.: ubi propius ventum est, utrimque magno clamore concurritur,; so ; .—Transf.: adversus has concurrentis belli minas, legati vallum murosque firmabant,—
Not in war; in the jurists, to make the same claim, enter into competition with: si non sit, qui ei concurrat, habeat solus bonorum possessionem,: in hereditatem fratri concurrere,: in pignus,: in pignore, ib.—
Trop. (rare): in tantā causarum varietate cum alia colligantur vel ipsa inter se concurrant, vel in diversum ambiguitate ducantur, : cum dolore,: concurrit illinc publica, hinc regis salus,.—
Of abstract objects (occurrences, circumstances, points of time, etc.), to meet, concur, fall out at the same time, happen: multa concurrunt simul,; so, concurrunt multae opiniones,: tot verisimilia,: res contrariae,: ista casu,: quae ut concurrant omnia, optabile est,: saepe concurrunt aliquorum bene de me meritorum inter ipsos contentiones,: si quid tale accidisset, ut non concurrerent nomina,that the reciprocal accounts do not meet, become due on the same day,; cf.: sponsalia in idem tempus,: concurrit actio legis Aquiliae et injuriarum,to have place together, to be coincident,.—
Pregn., to accord, agree with (in jurid. Lat.): concurrit cum veritate,: cum summā,.

la:noun:concursus.html:
concursus, ūs, m.
concurro

In partic., absol., an uproar, tumult: quem concursum in oppido factum putatis? quem clamorem?; cf. : quive coetu, concursu, turbā, seditione incendium fecerit,; pr.—
A running or dashing together, a pressing, striking one upon another, an encountering, meeting; a concourse, etc.
Of corporeal objects.
In gen.: concursus, motus, etc. (corporum quorundam) efficiunt ignes,; cf.: concursu suo nubes excussere semina ignis,; cf. also : caeli,: fortuito (atomorum),; : navium,; ; : lunae et solis,conjunction,: oris, a shutting (v. concurro, II. A. 1.), Spald.: asper verborum,a harsh combination,: extremorum verborum cum insequentibus,: vocalium,: quinque amnium in unum confluens,.—
Esp., milit. t. t., an onset, attack, charge: utriusque exercitus,; ; : acerrimo concursu pugnare,; ; ; ; et saep.: proelii,.—
Transf.
Concursus omnium philosophorum sustinere, assaults, .—

est, ; ; Gai .—

Trop.
To take or seize something by the sense of sight, to see, perceive (cf. comprehendo, II. A.): haec tanta oculis bona concipio,.—Far more freq.,
To perceive in mind.
In gen., to comprehend intellectually, to take in, imagine, conceive, think: agedum, inaugura fierine possit, quod nunc ego mente concipio,; so, aliquid animo,; cf.: imaginem quandam concipere animo perfecti oratoris,; cf. ; : quid mirum si in auspiciis imbecilli animi superstitiosa ista concipiant?: quantalibet magnitudo hominis concipiatur animo, Drak. ad loc.: de aliquo summa concipere,: onus operis opinione prima concipere,: protinus concepit Italiam et arma virumque, conceived the plan of the Æneid, .—
In partic., to understand, comprehend, perceive: quoniam principia rerum omnium animo ac mente conceperit,: quae neque concipi animo nisi ab iis qui videre, neque, etc.,: fragor, qui concipi humanā mente non potest,: concipere animo potes, quam simus fatigati,.—With acc. and inf.: quod ita juratum est, ut mens conciperet fleri oportere, id servandum est,: forsitan et lucos illic concipias animo esse,: concepit, eos homines posse jure mulceri,; fin.—
To receive in one's self, adopt, harbor any disposition of mind, emotion, passion, evil design, etc., to give place to, foster, to take in, receive; to commit (the figure derived from the absorbing of liquids; hence): quod non solum vitia concipiunt ipsi, sed ea infundunt in civitatem,: inimicitiae et aedilitate et praeturā conceptae,; so, mente vaticinos furores,: animo ingentes iras,: spem,; cf.: spemque metumque,: aliquid spe,: amorem,: pectore tantum robur,: auribus tantam cupiditatem,: re publicā violandā fraudis inexpiabiles concipere,: malum aut scelus,: scelus in sese,: flagitium cum aliquo,.—
To draw up, comprise, express something in words, to compose (cf. comprehendo, II. C.): quod ex animi tui sententiā juraris, sicut verbis concipiatur more nostro,: vadimonium, (15), 3: jusjurandum,; ; cf.: jurisjurandi verba,; and verba,: edictum,: libellos,: stipulationem,: obligationem in futurum,: actionem in bonum et aequum,: foedus, (id est conceptis verbis: concepta autem verba dicuntur jurandi formula, quam nobis transgredi non licet, Serv.): audet tamen Antias Valerius concipere summas (of the slain, etc.),to report definitely,.—T. t., of the lang. of religion, to make something (as a festival, auspices, war, etc.) known, to promulgate, declare in a set form of words, to designate formally: ubi viae competunt tum in competis sacrificatur: quotannis is dies (sc.
